Orthopedic Trauma · Resident Education

Humeral Shaft Fractures

Diaphyseal humerus — OTA/AO 12-A, B, C

Rockwood & Green 10th Ed. Ch. 37 AO Foundation Surgery Reference
Epidemiology & Mechanism

Overview

  • Account for approximately 3–5% of all fractures
  • Bimodal: young males (high-energy) and elderly females (low-energy/osteoporotic)
  • Middle third most common (60%), proximal third (30%), distal third (10%)
  • Majority (>90%) heal with nonoperative management

Mechanism of Injury

  • Direct blow — transverse or comminuted pattern
  • Indirect torsional — spiral pattern (arm wrestling, throwing)
  • High-energy — MVA, gunshot; higher comminution, open fracture risk
  • Pathological — lytic lesion/metastasis; suspect in low-energy spiral

Deforming Forces by Level

Fracture LevelProximal FragmentDistal Fragment
Above pectoralis majorAbducted + ER (deltoid, rotator cuff)Adducted + proximally displaced (pec major)
Below pec major, above deltoidAdducted (pec major)Abducted (deltoid)
Below deltoid insertionAbducted + ER (deltoid)Proximally displaced (biceps, triceps)
Tolerance for Malalignment (Rockwood & Green)
Up to 20° anterior angulation, 30° varus/valgus, and 3 cm shortening are generally well-tolerated. Rotational malalignment >15° is cosmetically and functionally significant.

Initial Evaluation

  • AP and lateral radiographs of entire humerus including shoulder and elbow
  • Neurovascular exam mandatory — document radial nerve function (wrist/finger extension)
  • ATLS protocol for high-energy trauma
  • CT for intra-articular extension or suspected pathological fracture
Surgical Anatomy

Anatomy & Neurovascular Considerations

Figure 37-9 · Rockwood & Green 10th Ed — Neurovascular anatomy of the upper arm

Radial Nerve — The Critical Structure

Figure 37-4 · Rockwood & Green 10th Ed — Holstein-Lewis fracture with radial nerve at risk
  • Posterior cord (C5–C8, T1); enters posterior compartment via triangular space with profunda brachii
  • Traverses the spiral groove from medial to lateral, posterior to the humerus
  • Pierces the lateral intermuscular septum ~10 cm proximal to the lateral epicondyle
  • Most vulnerable at the distal third–middle third junction
  • Holstein-Lewis fracture: spiral fracture of distal third with radial nerve trapped at lateral intermuscular septum — higher exploration rate
⚠ Radial Nerve Injury
Primary radial nerve palsy: ~11% overall, up to ~22% for spiral/distal-third fractures. Majority (>70%) are neurapraxia recovering spontaneously at 3–4 months. EMG/NCS at 6–8 weeks if no recovery. Explore if: open fracture, Holstein-Lewis pattern, no recovery by 3–4 months, post-reduction palsy.

Key Nerves by Approach

Posterior Approach

  • Radial nerve + profunda brachii — in spiral groove
  • Ulnar nerve — medial, behind medial intermuscular septum
  • Axillary nerve — proximal; safe zone >5 cm from greater tuberosity

Anterolateral Approach

  • Radial nerve — crosses at lateral intermuscular septum ~10 cm above lateral epicondyle
  • Musculocutaneous nerve — lateral to brachialis
  • Lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve — protect distally

Anteromedial Approach

  • Brachial artery — medial, must protect throughout
  • Median nerve — travels with brachial artery
  • Ulnar nerve — posterior to medial intermuscular septum

Compartments

  • Anterior: biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis; musculocutaneous nerve
  • Posterior: triceps (3 heads); radial nerve
  • Lateral intermuscular septum separates compartments

Treatment Principles

Management

Nonoperative Management

AO Principle — Nonoperative First-Line
Union rates of 94–98% with functional bracing (Sarmiento). Acceptable alignment: <20° sagittal, <30° coronal angulation, <3 cm shortening.

Nonoperative Protocol

  • 0–1 week: Coaptation splint or hanging arm cast with collar-and-cuff sling
  • Week 1–3: Transition to functional (Sarmiento) brace once swelling resolves
  • Brace wear: 8–12 weeks typical; pendulum exercises from day 1
  • Upright posture essential — gravity aids alignment
  • Serial radiographs at 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12 weeks

Indications

Nonoperative

  • Isolated closed fracture within acceptable alignment
  • Transverse, oblique, or spiral patterns
  • Patient compliance with bracing
  • Low-energy mechanism

Surgical Indications

  • Open fracture
  • Vascular injury
  • Ipsilateral forearm fracture (floating elbow)
  • Bilateral humeral fractures
  • Segmental fracture
  • Polytrauma / chest wall injury
  • Unacceptable alignment after closed reduction
  • Pathological fracture
  • Periprosthetic fracture
  • Radial nerve palsy with indication for exploration
  • Intra-articular extension

Surgical Options

MethodIndicationsAdvantagesDisadvantages
Plate ORIFMost fractures requiring surgery; distal third; radial nerve explorationDirect visualization, excellent stability, nerve accessLarger exposure, plate removal
IM NailMiddle-third transverse, segmental, pathologicalMinimally invasive, load-sharing, good for osteoporosisShoulder impingement (antegrade); elbow stiffness (retrograde); no radial nerve access
External FixationDamage control, contaminated open fractures, vascular temporizationRapid application, allows soft tissue managementPin-tract infection, temporary
HUMMER Trial (AO Foundation)
Randomized trial comparing IM nail vs. plate fixation showed no significant difference in union rates; AO currently favors plate fixation as the standard surgical method for most diaphyseal humeral fractures.

Fixation Principles (AO)

  • Minimum 6 cortices proximal and distal to fracture for plate fixation
  • Broad/narrow 4.5 mm DCP or LC-DCP; locking plates for osteoporotic bone
  • Lag screw for spiral/oblique patterns (>2× bone diameter fracture length)
  • Bridge plating for comminuted patterns — do not attempt reduction of individual small fragments
  • Antegrade IM nail: entry point at greater tuberosity tip; avoid supraspinatus insertion
Surgical Approaches

Approach Walkthrough

Posterior Approach
Workhorse approach. Full diaphysis access. Patient prone or lateral. Radial nerve must be identified.
Step 1 of 8
Anterolateral Approach
Proximal and middle-third fractures. Extensile proximally (deltopectoral) and distally. Radial nerve identified at lateral intermuscular septum.
Step 1 of 6
Anteromedial Approach
Medial diaphysis access. Useful for medially-based fractures and brachial artery exploration. Beware median nerve, brachial artery, and ulnar nerve.

Complications & Outcomes

Complications

Nonunion

  • Rate: ~2–5% with functional bracing; higher with some surgical series
  • Risk factors: distraction at fracture site, inadequate immobilization, smoking, obesity, transverse pattern, distal-third location
  • Definition: failure to achieve union by 6 months (AO)
  • Treatment: compression plating + autograft (iliac crest) ± exchange nailing
⚠ Hanging Arm Cast — Nonunion Risk
Hanging arm casts can cause distraction at the fracture site, increasing nonunion risk. Functional bracing (Sarmiento) is preferred after the acute phase.

Radial Nerve Palsy

  • Most common nerve injury: ~11% overall, up to 22% distal third
  • Spontaneous recovery in >70% at 3–4 months
  • Management: dynamic wrist/finger extension splint; EMG at 6–8 weeks
  • Explore if: open fracture, Holstein-Lewis, no recovery by 3–4 months, post-reduction palsy
  • Iatrogenic injury: ~2–5%; mostly neurapraxia

Surgical Complications

ComplicationRateNotes
Plate fixation — infection~2–3%Higher for open fractures
IM nail — shoulder pain (antegrade)~10–20%Rotator cuff impingement at entry point
IM nail — elbow pain (retrograde)~10%Triceps splitting entry
Iatrogenic nerve injury~2–5%Radial nerve most common; usually neurapraxia
Re-fracture after plate removalSignificantDelay removal >18 months; stress riser at screw holes

Expected Outcomes

  • Nonoperative union rate: 94–98% with functional bracing (Sarmiento series)
  • Return to full function: 3–6 months for most patients
  • Shoulder and elbow ROM generally well-preserved with functional bracing
  • Plate fixation: union ~95%; allows earlier mobilization
  • Pathological fractures: IM nail preferred; prophylactic fixation for impending fractures
